title: Why the Great Salt Lake is two colors
subtitle: Great Salt Lake · Utah
deck: From orbit, Utah’s Great Salt Lake can look painted in two pigments — pink-red on one side of a thin line, blue-green on the other. The line is a railroad causeway. The colors are what happens when one lake is forced to become two chemistries.
shortDescription: A railroad causeway, restricted exchange, and salinity that split one lake into two living colors.
seoTitle: Why the Great Salt Lake Is Two Colors — Causeway, Salinity & Microbes — Deep Forest Dispatch
metaDescription: Why Utah’s Great Salt Lake looks half pink and half blue: the railroad causeway, restricted water exchange, salinity contrast, and the microbes that tint each arm.

location.name: Great Salt Lake
location.region: Northern Utah · remnant of Lake Bonneville

sections.heading: A lake with a hard edge

blocks.html: The Great Salt Lake does not fade from one color into another. On many clear days, the change is abrupt: a north arm that reads pink to red, a south arm that reads greener or blue-green, and a narrow east–west seam between them.

That seam is not a trick of the camera. It is infrastructure. A rock-fill railroad causeway has restricted water exchange across the lake since 1959 — long enough for salinity, biology, and color to diverge.

blocks.alt: Oblique orbital view of Great Salt Lake’s two-tone waters and surrounding Bonneville landscape
blocks.caption: From the International Space Station, the color contrast and the east–west causeway alignment are unmistakable.

blocks.html: The Great Salt Lake sits in northern Utah as a shallow terminal lake: water arrives from rivers, streams, precipitation, and groundwater, and leaves mainly by evaporation. It is a remnant of much larger Ice Age Lake Bonneville.
Today’s main body is commonly described as a north arm (Gunnison Bay) and a south arm (Gilbert Bay), separated by the causeway that carries rail across the lake.

blocks.caption: Great Salt Lake between the Wasatch Front and the West Desert — a closed basin where salt has nowhere else to go.

sections.heading: How the causeway remade the lake

blocks.html: Before the mid-twentieth-century rock-fill causeway, the lake mixed more freely. Completing the causeway in 1959 partitioned the main body into two basins with only limited connection — historically through culverts, porous fill, and later engineered openings and a bridge span.

Restricted exchange matters because freshwater does not arrive evenly. The Bear, Weber, and Jordan rivers deliver the great majority of streamflow into the south arm. The north arm receives far less direct freshwater and tends to concentrate salt.
Utah Geological Survey and USGS accounts treat the causeway as the decisive human alteration that produced the modern salinity split — not a cosmetic shoreline feature.

With most freshwater locked on the south side, the north arm commonly sits at much higher salinity — often near saturation with respect to halite (rock salt). The south arm remains hypersaline by ocean standards, but typically far less extreme than the north.

Peer-reviewed water-and-salt modeling of the lake has reported multi-decadal averages on the order of roughly 300+ g/L in the north versus much lower values in the south — numbers that move with lake level, season, and how open the causeway connections are. Treat them as evidence of a persistent gradient, not a permanent barcode.
Dense north-arm brine can also move through deeper openings and influence stratification in the south. The physical story is exchange under constraint — not a complete seal.

sections.heading: Why the colors follow the chemistry

blocks.html: Salinity selects the biology. In the hypersaline north arm, salt-tolerant communities — including the green alga Dunaliella salina and halophilic archaea such as Halobacterium — can dominate. Their red carotenoid pigments help the water read pink to red from above.

In the less extreme south arm, greener algal communities (often including Dunaliella viridis) are more typical, and the water’s color shifts accordingly. Brine shrimp and brine flies are part of the same salinity-shaped food web, especially in the south.

blocks.alt: ISS detail of the reddish north arm of Great Salt Lake
blocks.caption: North of the causeway, high salinity and pigmented microbes can paint the water a pronounced red.

blocks.html: So the honest chain is physical first: causeway → restricted exchange → salinity divergence → different microbial communities → visible color contrast. “Bacteria on one side” is a fragment of the last step, not the system.
This diagram compresses the system into the sequence a satellite already shows: a barrier, two chemistries, and two living colors.

blocks.alt: Diagram of Great Salt Lake north and south arms divided by a railroad causeway with salinity and microbial color keys
Annotated NASA photograph highlighting the Great Salt Lake causeway and color contrast
blocks.caption: Same physics on the real photograph: the causeway is the hinge of the color story.

sections.heading: Why the colors are not permanent paint

blocks.html: Lake level rises and falls with climate and water use. Culverts have been closed; openings and a bridge have changed exchange. North-arm salt crusts thicken and dissolve. Microbial blooms wax and wane with season and chemistry.
That is why some years look like a hard two-tone flag and other years look softer or shifted. The causeway still structures the system; the exact pigments are weather and management written on water.
USGS satellite histories of Great Salt Lake make the same point across decades: the divide is durable, the appearance is not fixed.

If you visit the Wasatch Front, high-contrast lake light rewards patience — and honest conditions matter as much as the postcard. Waypoint’s Dashboard and Scenes are built for checking weather and light before you go, not for inventing a lake-color forecast.
